title: Being Wrong Less
coreMove: Take a tempting conclusion apart into first-principles assumptions, then design the smallest test that can expose the unforced error cheaply.
sourcePressure: The source frames better thinking as being wrong less: reduce unforced errors, reason from first principles, preserve useful antifragile stress, de-risk commitment, and use MVP tests before scaling.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Treating error reduction as timid delay instead of active, low-cost contact with reality.

sourceAnchors.name: tennis unforced error
sourceAnchors.detail: the source uses tennis to distinguish a self-created miss from a shot nobody could have returned
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The missed easy return matters because no opponent had to be brilliant; the mistake came from your side of the net.

sourceAnchors.name: minimum viable product
sourceAnchors.detail: the source supports testing cheaply before overcommitting so the downside stays low
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: A stripped-down version gives reality a vote before your confidence gets a budget.

hook: You are probably wrong more often than you think
What if being right is the wrong goal?
A smart person knows they can be wrong
tryThisNow: Set a timer and list assumptions
examples: warehouse rollout copied from old examples

exampleSpecs.domain: Sarah, a museum exhibit lead choosing whether to rebuild the ticketing kiosk flow after three angry visitor comments
exampleSpecs.audience: product-minded operators who overreact to vivid complaints
exampleSpecs.stakes: a six-week redesign could consume the education team’s launch window
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Sarah pins the three complaint slips beside the month’s visitor log, circles the exact assumption about frequency, and swaps the redesign pitch for a two-day lobby observation test
exampleSpecs.firstImage: three crumpled comment slips under a brass paperweight

exampleSpecs.domain: Daniel, a civil-engineering student checking a bridge-load answer that sounds elegant but rests on one borrowed formula
exampleSpecs.audience: students who mistake fluency for understanding
exampleSpecs.stakes: a lab grade and a later design review depend on whether he can rebuild the logic
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Daniel erases the polished solution, writes only the known loads and constraints, and finds the unsupported assumption before submitting the revision
exampleSpecs.firstImage: eraser crumbs collecting along the bottom of a calculation page

exampleSpecs.domain: Claire, a neighborhood bakery owner testing gluten-free demand before signing a lease for a second kitchen
exampleSpecs.audience: small-business readers facing a tempting leap
exampleSpecs.stakes: a lease would lock her into fixed costs before demand is proven
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Claire answers a friend’s smallest-real-test question by opening twenty preorder slots instead of calling the landlord
exampleSpecs.firstImage: “What would prove this before you rent another oven?”
mustAvoid: banned baking-business shell with quitting a job

exampleSpecs.domain: Étienne, a hospital lab supervisor piloting a specimen-tracking checklist on one shift before changing every ward handoff
exampleSpecs.audience: managers under pressure to scale a promising process
exampleSpecs.stakes: a hospital-wide change could slow urgent samples if the idea breaks
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Étienne watches the night-shift pilot expose one mislabeled handoff and revises the checklist before asking daytime wards to adopt it
exampleSpecs.firstImage: fluorescent light reflecting off a tray of barcode labels

exampleSpecs.domain: Aanya, a junior barrister deciding whether to ask one narrow courtroom question before committing to a full theory of the case
exampleSpecs.audience: professionals whose confidence can outrun evidence
exampleSpecs.stakes: a premature theory could waste limited cross-examination time
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Aanya writes the one fact that would collapse her theory, asks a narrow witness question, and lets the answer decide whether to proceed
exampleSpecs.firstImage: What fact would make the whole story buckle?

exampleSpecs.domain: Jonas, an amateur triathlete using a low-stakes brick workout to test a new race nutrition plan
exampleSpecs.audience: readers who avoid all stress and call it discipline
exampleSpecs.stakes: race day stomach trouble would be expensive, but a training test is survivable
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Jonas deliberately tests the drink mix during a short bike-run session, records the stomach reaction, and keeps the useful stress instead of hiding from it
exampleSpecs.firstImage: You can smell the citrus drink mix before the bottle is even full

tryThisNowSpec: Take one live decision and write the one assumption that would make it fail; shrink the next action until that assumption can meet reality today without major cost.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person direct address, retrospective, question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

skillTargets: identify the chapter-specific model in a fresh scenario for Being Wrong Less
choose the visible action that performs the core move rather than naming the concept
explain the failure mode that appears when the model is used generically
evaluate tradeoffs and limits without sliding into certainty, cynicism, or manipulation

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'
